name: Blossom
intro: Blossom is an open specification for storing and retrieving files on publicly accessible servers. It gives Nostr applications a shared way to work with images, video, and other binary data.

sections.title: A file, identified by its contents
sections.text: Blossom addresses files by their SHA-256 hash and uses Nostr keys for identity. Its HTTP endpoints cover retrieval, uploads, and management; additional specifications describe mirroring and other capabilities.

sections.title: Infrastructure other projects can build on
sections.text: The archive places Blossom in SEC-01, alongside Blossom Drive. Nsite uses Blossom servers to store the files of a static website: one project becoming a foundation for another.

name: Nutzaps
intro: Nutzaps bring Cashu ecash into Nostr interactions. They let applications send and receive value through the same open network used for social messages.

sections.title: Wallets and payments, working together
sections.text: NIP-60 describes Cashu wallets on Nostr. NIP-61 describes nutzaps: ecash-based payments attached to people or events. Together, they provide common building blocks for clients integrating ecash.

sections.title: From a standard to everyday clients
sections.text: Both specifications appear in the SEC-02 archive. Later work, including Wallnut in SEC-07, explores these flows inside Nostr applications.

name: Wikifreedia
intro: Wikifreedia is a Nostr-native wiki that makes room for multiple perspectives. It explores how shared knowledge can live on an open protocol rather than depend on one central publishing platform.

sections.title: A wiki with room for disagreement
sections.text: The project embraces multiple perspectives instead of enforcing a single canonical account. Its work became part of NIP-54, a specification for wiki-style content on Nostr.

sections.title: Built at SEC-01
sections.text: Wikifreedia appears in the first organized cohort’s archive, alongside Blossom and Zapstore. Its focus is publishing and discovering knowledge on a network people can build on.

name: Nsite
intro: Nsite publishes static websites using Nostr and Blossom. Website files live on Blossom servers, while Nostr events provide the mapping needed to find them.

sections.title: Two open building blocks
sections.text: Blossom supplies file storage. Nostr supplies the publishing layer that maps a site to its files. Together they offer a different route for putting static websites online.

sections.title: One cohort’s work becomes another’s foundation
sections.text: Nsite is archived under SEC-02. It builds on Blossom, which appeared in SEC-01, showing how shared infrastructure continues to grow between cohorts.

name: TollGate
intro: TollGate brings bearer payments to network access. It combines payment handling, captive portal access control, and gateway discovery so people can buy connectivity in small increments.

sections.title: Pay for access, as you need it
sections.text: The archived system includes Merchant for ecash payments, Valve for access control, Crows Nest for gateway discovery, and Janitor for updates. The work connects payments to the actual delivery of a network resource.

sections.title: The roots of FIPS
sections.text: TollGate appears in SEC-02, with captive portal work continuing in SEC-07. Its networking work also spawned FIPS, which explores the peer-to-peer connections underneath applications.

name: Zapstore
intro: Zapstore is a permissionless app store powered by open standards and your social graph. It connects software distribution with the identities and relationships people already use on Nostr.

sections.title: Software distribution on an open network
sections.text: Instead of treating app discovery as a closed platform, Zapstore uses Nostr-native social identity as part of how software is published and discovered.

sections.title: From SEC-01 into the world
sections.text: Zapstore is one of the projects in the SEC-01 archive. On our homepage, the dandelion is its image: apps as seeds, able to travel beyond the place where they started.

name: FIPS
tagline: An encrypted mesh across any medium.
intro: FIPS—the Free Internetworking Peering System—is a self-organizing, encrypted peer-to-peer mesh. It connects peers over different kinds of transport, giving applications a network that can take more than one path.

sections.title: Different transports. One mesh.
sections.text: FIPS supports transports including Bluetooth, Ethernet, UDP, Tor, and serial links. Connections are encrypted between peers, with encryption at each hop. Existing IP applications can use its network interface.

sections.title: Grown from TollGate
sections.text: FIPS emerged from TollGate’s networking work. The SEC-05 archive includes its early prototype; SEC-07 expanded the work into Android nodes, endpoint discovery, routing research, learning tools, and more.

sections.title: A network that organizes itself
sections.text: Peers discover one another, form links, and reroute as the network changes. Identity comes from locally generated keys. The aim is connectivity that can grow wherever peers can exchange packets.

name: Nostr
tagline: A shared language for open networks.
intro: Nostr is an open protocol for publishing and exchanging signed messages through relays. People use cryptographic keys as their identity, so applications can share a common foundation without sharing one central operator.

sections.title: Keys, clients, and relays
sections.text: A client signs an event with your key and sends it to relays. Other clients request events and check their signatures. Relays store and deliver messages; your identity comes from your key. You can publish to several relays and use different clients.

sections.title: More than a social feed
sections.text: The same event format can support many kinds of applications. Blossom uses Nostr keys to authorize file operations. Nsite uses events to describe websites. Zapstore applies this shared identity layer to software distribution.

sections.title: A foundation for building together
sections.text: For our cohorts, Nostr is common ground: builders can connect new ideas to existing identities, applications, and infrastructure. Explore the related projects to see the different directions that work can take.

name: eCash
tagline: Value that travels like a message.
intro: Ecash is digital bearer money. Here we focus on Cashu, an open protocol for Chaumian ecash on Bitcoin. Wallets hold tokens issued by a mint, and those tokens can move through the same channels we use to exchange information.

sections.title: Privacy through blind signatures
sections.text: A mint issues tokens using blind signatures, which keep it from directly linking token issuance to later redemption. A recipient exchanges received tokens with the mint for fresh ones, preventing the same tokens from being spent again.

sections.title: A building block for payments
sections.text: Cashu tokens can be carried as text, making them useful inside messages and applications. Nutzaps connects ecash payments to Nostr events. TollGate applies bearer payments to network access.

sections.title: The mint’s role
sections.text: Tokens are claims on the issuing mint. Holders depend on that mint to redeem them; the privacy mechanism does not remove this trust. This model gives builders a distinct set of tradeoffs to understand when designing a payment flow.

name: MLS
intro: Messaging Layer Security is an open standard for end-to-end encrypted group communication. It lets a group establish and update shared cryptographic keys as people join, leave, and exchange messages.

sections.title: Keeping up with a changing group
sections.text: Group conversations need more than encryption for a single pair of people. MLS coordinates changes in membership and keys, allowing members to send protected messages without separately encrypting every message for every other participant.

sections.title: Keys that move forward
sections.text: MLS is designed to protect earlier messages if a current key is exposed, and to restore protection for future messages after appropriate key updates. These properties are called forward secrecy and post-compromise security.

sections.title: From standard to application
sections.text: MLS supplies a cryptographic foundation. Applications still need identity, delivery, and a usable interface. Marmot brings MLS together with Nostr identities, while MDK provides implementation tools for building on Marmot.

name: Marmot
intro: Marmot is a protocol for end-to-end encrypted group messaging. It combines Nostr public keys for identity with Messaging Layer Security for group key agreement, giving builders a shared foundation for private conversations.

sections.title: Bring identity and encryption together
sections.text: Nostr supplies an identity people can use across applications. MLS handles the cryptographic state of a changing group. Marmot specifies how these pieces work together, including how application content is represented inside encrypted messages.

sections.title: Delivery without a single point of dependence
sections.text: Marmot clients can exchange messages through Nostr relays, with redundant delivery so a group need not depend on one endpoint. The protocol separates delivery from identity and encryption, allowing other transports to be used as well.

sections.title: Build on the shared protocol
sections.text: MDK implements Marmot for application developers. Our archive also includes experiments with MLS on Nostr and Marmot Chat: places to explore how these foundations are being used.

name: MDK
tagline: From messaging protocol to working code.
intro: The Marmot Development Kit is a Rust implementation of the Marmot protocol. It gives developers reusable components for encrypted group messaging, connecting the protocol’s rules to the code an application needs.

sections.title: The machinery behind the conversation
sections.text: MDK uses OpenMLS for group key agreement and manages the state that changes as a conversation evolves. Its workspace includes storage and integration components so applications can preserve that state between sessions.

sections.title: Connect it to an application
sections.text: Transport adapters connect the messaging engine to delivery networks such as Nostr. Bindings and application integration layers let builders use the shared implementation while developing their own interfaces and experiences.

sections.title: Understand the layers
sections.text: Start with MLS for the encryption model, Marmot for the messaging protocol, and Nostr for identity and relay-based delivery. MDK brings those foundations into an implementation that builders can work with.
